# The Tale of the River Eternal

In the time before time, two villages stood on opposite banks of the River Eternal. The Upstream Village received fresh water each day, while the Downstream Village struggled with drought.

The Water-Keeper of the Upstream Village faced a choice: hoard the precious water or release it downstream. The spirits had blessed the water with a peculiar magic—whatever was sent downstream would triple in abundance as it flowed.

The first Water-Keeper, moved by compassion, sent one-third of their water downstream. The spirits blessed this generosity, and the water multiplied. The grateful Downstream Village, now flourishing, sent back gifts of grain and fish—sometimes equal to what they'd received, sometimes more, sometimes less.

Over seasons, a rhythm emerged. When Water-Keepers sent generously, the downstream village prospered and returned abundance. When they withheld from fear, both villages suffered—for the magic only worked through trust.

The wisest Water-Keepers learned that sending freely created prosperity for all. Even when returns varied like the phases of the moon, the act of giving itself invited reciprocity. The river taught them: abundance flows to those who trust it to flow, and communities flourish when each considers the other's needs as important as their own.

Thus the villages thrived, forever linked by the River Eternal.

# The Tale of the River Eternal

In the time before time, two villages stood on opposite banks of the River Eternal. The Upstream Village received fresh water each day, while the Downstream Village struggled with drought.

The Water-Keeper of the Upstream Village faced a choice: hoard the precious water or release it downstream. The spirits had blessed the water with a peculiar magic—whatever was sent downstream would triple in abundance as it flowed.

The first Water-Keeper, moved by compassion, sent one-third of their water downstream. The spirits blessed this generosity, and the water multiplied. The grateful Downstream Village, now flourishing, sent back gifts of grain and fish—sometimes equal to what they'd received, sometimes more, sometimes less.
